detail: A compulsory liquidation can be initiated if the company passes a special resolution for winding up by the court, as per Section 122(1) of the Insolvency Act 1986.
verified_quote: A company may be wound up by the court if— (a) the company has by special resolution resolved that the company be wound up by the court,
notes: Section 122(1)(a) of the Insolvency Act 1986 explicitly states this as a circumstance in which a company may be wound up by the court.

detail: A compulsory liquidation can be initiated if the court deems it 'just and equitable' for the company to be wound up, as per Section 122(1) of the Insolvency Act 1986.
verified_quote: A company may be wound up by the court if—(g) the court is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up.
notes: Section 122(1)(g) of the Insolvency Act 1986 confirms that a company can be wound up by the court if it is deemed 'just and equitable'.

detail: An unpaid judgment debt is a typical way to evidence a company's inability to pay its debts for a winding-up petition.
verified_quote: A company is deemed unable to pay its debts—... (b) if execution or other process issued on a judgment, decree or order of any court in favour of a creditor is returned unsatisfied in whole or in part; or ... (e) if it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that the company is unable to pay its debts as they fall due.
notes: The quote is from Section 123 of the Insolvency Act 1986, which defines 'inability to pay debts' for the purpose of winding up a company. The GOV.UK guidance also lists a court judgment as evidence of money owed for a winding-up petition.

detail: A deposit of £2,600 must be paid to the Official Receiver when a winding-up petition is filed.
verified_quote: The fees are: £343 - court fees; £2,600 - petition deposit (to manage the 'winding-up'). A petition may not be filed unless— (a)a receipt for the deposit payable to the official receiver is produced on presentation of the petition. Unless the petition is one in respect of which rule 7.7(2)(b) of the Insolvency Rules applies, a winding up petition will not be treated as having been presented until the Court fee and official receiver's deposit have been paid.
notes: The GOV.UK website confirms the £2,600 petition deposit. The Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016 (Rule 7.7) and the Practice Direction – Insolvency Proceedings – Civil Procedure Rules (Section 9.3.1) establish the requirement for this deposit to be paid to the Official Receiver when a winding-up petition is filed. The increase to £2,600 for creditors' winding-up petitions took effect from 1 November 2022.

detail: The total initial outlay for the petitioning creditor in a compulsory liquidation can be in the range of £3,500 to £4,000.
verified_quote: The fees are: £343 - court fees. £2,600 - petition deposit (to manage the 'winding-up').
notes: According to official GOV.UK guidance, the mandatory court fee for a winding-up petition is £343 and the petition deposit to the Official Receiver is £2,600. These two fixed costs alone total £2,943. The 'total initial outlay' for a petitioning creditor would also include other essential disbursements such as process server fees (typically £100-£200 plus VAT) and the cost of advertising the petition in The London Gazette (approximately £80-£120 plus VAT). Furthermore, solicitors' professional fees for preparing, issuing, and progressing the petition are a significant component of the initial outlay, with estimates for drafting alone ranging from £1,500 to £2,000 plus VAT for a non-complex case, or general legal costs between £1,000 and £5,000. Even with the lowest estimates for these additional costs (e.g., £100 for process server, £80 for advertising, and a conservative £1,000 for initial legal fees), the total initial outlay would be approximately £2,943 + £100 + £80 + £1,000 = £4,123. This sum exceeds the upper end of the claimed range of £3,500 to £4,000. The Official Receiver's deposit was increased from £1,600 to £2,600 from 1 November 2022.

detail: The Official Receiver charges statutory fees including an administration fee of £5,000 and a general fee of £6,000 for winding-up by the court.
verified_quote: Winding up by the court other than a winding up on a petition presented under section 124A – official receiver's administration fee. On the making of a winding-up order, other than on a petition presented under section 124A, for the performance of the official receiver's duties as official receiver, including the duty to investigate and report on the affairs of bodies in liquidation, the fee of— [F3£6,000]. Official receiver's general fee. On the making of a bankruptcy order or the making of a winding up order by the court for the costs not recovered out of the official receiver's administration fee of administering— (a) bankruptcy orders, (b) winding up orders made by the court the fee of— [F5£7,200].
notes: The claim states an administration fee of £5,000 and a general fee of £6,000. According to The Insolvency Proceedings (Fees) Order 2016, as amended by The Insolvency Proceedings (Fees) (Amendment) Order 2024, which came into force on 9 January 2025, the Official Receiver's administration fee for winding up by the court (other than a petition presented under section 124A) is £6,000. The Official Receiver's general fee is £7,200. The original fees of £5,000 for the administration fee and £6,000 for the general fee were applicable prior to the 2025 amendment.

detail: The overall cost for a compulsory liquidation process can be between £1,000 and £7,500, depending on the company's size and complexity.
verified_quote: The OR's administration fee for winding up by the court other than a winding up on a petition presented under section 124A Insolvency Act 1986 will increase from £5,000 to £6,000. The OR's general fee will increase from £6,000 to £7,200.
notes: The Insolvency Proceedings (Fees) (Amendment) Order 2024, effective from 9 January 2025, significantly updated the fees for compulsory liquidation. The Official Receiver's administration fee for a general winding up by the court is £6,000, and the Official Receiver's general fee is £7,200. These two mandatory fees alone total £13,200. Additional costs, such as the court fee (£280 or £343) and the petition deposit (£2,600), further increase the overall cost, demonstrating that the minimum statutory fees for compulsory liquidation far exceed the claimed range of £1,000 to £7,500.

detail: For misfeasance claims (Section 212 IA 1986), a liquidator or even a creditor with court leave can apply to the court.
verified_quote: The court may, on the application of the official receiver or the liquidator, or of any creditor or contributory, examine into the conduct of the person falling within subsection (1)... The power of a contributory to make an application under subsection (3) is not exercisable except with the leave of the court...
notes: Section 212(3) of the Insolvency Act 1986 states that the court may hear an application from 'the official receiver or the liquidator, or of any creditor or contributory'. Section 212(5) specifies that 'The power of a contributory to make an application under subsection (3) is not exercisable except with the leave of the court'. Therefore, a liquidator can apply. A creditor can also apply. However, the requirement for 'court leave' is explicitly stated in the legislation for a *contributory*, but not for a *creditor*. As such, the claim is partially verified because a liquidator and a creditor can apply, but the condition of 'with court leave' for a creditor is not explicitly stated in the primary legislation for creditors, unlike for contributories.

detail: Fraudulent trading (Section 213 IA 1986) is a criminal offence that can lead to an unlimited fine and a prison sentence of up to 10 years.
verified_quote: A person guilty of an offence under this section is liable— (a) on conviction on indictment, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years or a fine (or both);
notes: The claim is partially verified. Fraudulent trading is indeed a criminal offence that can lead to an unlimited fine and a prison sentence of up to 10 years. However, this criminal offence and its penalties are stipulated under Section 993 of the Companies Act 2006, not Section 213 of the Insolvency Act 1986. Section 213 of the Insolvency Act 1986 deals with the civil liability aspect of fraudulent trading, allowing for contributions to a company's assets. The fine is 'unlimited' on conviction on indictment as no upper limit is specified in the legislation for this type of conviction.

verified_quote: A disqualification order usually carries with it an order to pay the costs and expenses of the Secretary of State.
notes: This quote is from official GOV.UK guidance on the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986.

detail: Breaching a director disqualification order or undertaking is a criminal offence, potentially leading to a fine, up to 2 years in prison, and personal liability for company debts incurred during that period.
verified_quote: Anyone contravening a disqualification order or undertaking is committing a criminal offence and can be fined and/or sent to prison for up to 2 years. They could also be disqualified for a further period. When someone contravenes an order or undertaking, they might also become personally liable for any debts of a company that are incurred during that period.
notes: This information is provided by GOV.UK, specifically within guidance related to the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986.

detail: A compensation order may also be made against a disqualified director to repay losses suffered by creditors.

HMRC can issue Personal Liability Notices (PLNs) to directors if they are deemed to have intentionally or recklessly failed to ensure the company paid PAYE, National Insurance, or Construction Industry Scheme deductions.

It is a criminal offence for a director of a company that has gone into insolvent liquidation to re-use the company name (or a name so similar as to suggest an association) for another business within 5 years without court permission (Sections 216 & 217 Insolvency Act 1986), potentially making them personally liable for the debts of the new company.
Directors of a liquidated company are banned for 5 years from forming, managing or promoting any business with the same or a similar name to their liquidated company, subject to certain exceptions.
For transactions at an undervalue (Section 238 IA 1986), insolvency is presumed if the transaction occurred within two years before insolvency.

Directors' general duties are set out in Sections 171-177 of the Companies Act 2006, including duties to act within powers, promote the success of the company, exercise independent judgment, and exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence.
The Supreme Court's 'creditor duty' confirmed that directors must consider, and give effect to, the interests of creditors when insolvency is probable or inevitable.
Preferential creditors in a compulsory liquidation primarily include certain employee claims and a portion of HMRC debts (for certain taxes like VAT and PAYE, classified as secondary preferential).
Secured creditors holding floating charges are paid after liquidation costs and preferential creditors, from the remaining unencumbered assets, in a compulsory liquidation.
A Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL) process can be relatively quick, sometimes as fast as 8 days, compared to compulsory liquidation.
In Administration, the administrator must present their proposals to creditors within 8 weeks of appointment.
In Administration, directors must provide a Statement of Company's Affairs within 11 days of the administrator's appointment.
A standalone moratorium, introduced by the Corporate Insolvency and Governance Act 2020 (CIGA 2020), offers a 'breathing space' for companies in financial difficulty to explore rescue options.
The initial period for a standalone moratorium (under CIGA 2020) is 20 business days, which directors can extend for a further 20 business days without creditor consent.
A standalone moratorium can be extended for a maximum period of 364 days by court application.

For a Members' Voluntary Liquidation (MVL), a majority of directors must make a formal Declaration of Solvency no more than five weeks before the shareholders pass a special resolution to wind up the company.
For Company Dissolution (Voluntary Strike-Off), if no objections are raised within two months of submitting Form DS01, the company is struck off.
